summary: The things that attack you: a spider, a hound, a bull fighter. A creature body on its own rig, seen small and close.
why: A profile of its own rather than borrowing npc's, though the numbers come out the same,
and the reason is that they are the same by measurement rather than by inheritance. An
NPC and a monster share the situation - a painted figure on a page, seen from a few
metres, not tiling - so they share the answer. What they do not share is the default
material, and that is the field a profile exists to hold.
It is emphatically not world. Scenery is tiling art on large flat faces seen at a
distance, upscaled with the drawn model at full strength and padded by wrapping. A
monster's sheet is a body laid out on a page: it does not tile, and wrapped, the pixels
off one edge are fed back in as context from the other side of the animal.
Detail at 0.65 is armour's and is most of the point. These sheets are the smallest in the
project - the Spider's body is 64x64 and its legs are 32x64 - and the drawn model at full
strength turns a band of leg hair painted across four pixels into hard-edged rectangles
with dark outlines. The same setting protects a sword hilt from the same failure.
The 3x cap is the project's and is not negotiated down here even though these sheets are
tiny enough to tempt it. 32x64 taken to 96x192 is a reconstruction of 2,048 real pixels;
the same file at 8x would be a reconstruction of the same 2,048 pixels in a larger
container, which is the thing this pipeline was built to stop doing. See upscale.py.
Skin as the default rather than a shell or a hide, because a monster is a menagerie and a
default is what an unnamed slot falls to. What every one of them has in common is that it
is alive and dielectric, and skin is the version of that with no grain on it - the safe
way to be wrong, exactly as npc.json argues. What a creature is actually made of is said
per sheet: the Spider's two are chitin, and a Bull Fighter's axe will be steel.
The alternative was to file monsters under npc and let the directory decide. That reads
as a filing convenience until something needs to be true of every monster and of no
townsperson - which is already the case, because a monster has twelve fixed action slots
and a merchant has whatever its .bmd happens to hold. See viewer/Monsters.cs.
